title: Ten years, tens of millions of cells - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

As the Human Cell Atlas project enters its second decade, the question is no longer whether we can map human cells, it is what we will do with the map.

The Human Cell Atlas (HCA) consortium came to life in October 2016, when a group of around 100 researchers set the audacious goal of mapping every cell in the human body1. Led by Aviv Regev and Sarah Teichmann, the group aimed to create a comprehensive picture of the body’s ~30 trillion cells — how they differ, communicate, and change across health, disease and development. At the time, single-cell technologies were rapidly emerging, making it possible to characterize tens of thousands (eventually millions) of individual cells by their gene expression patterns and molecular features. Today, ten years later, the original vision has grown into one of the largest collaborative efforts in biology. Researchers have catalogued an extraordinary diversity of human cells, refined our understanding of familiar cell types and revealed previously unrecognized cell types, cellular states and populations. The project also established single-cell analysis as a foundational approach for studying human biology and developed many of the now commonly used methods for it. To accomplish the next stage — cataloguing billions instead of millions of cells — will build on more recent technological advances from spatial biology and AI.When the HCA was announced, single-cell technology was at a turning point. Smart-seq2 (ref. 2) and CEL-seq2 (ref. 3) had made single-cell transcriptomics more powerful and sensitive, and droplet-based sequencing using cellular barcodes enabled researchers to pool thousands of cells in a single experiment and computationally separate the reads afterward. By late 2016, it was possible to routinely quantify gene expression in tens of thousands of single cells with high accuracy at manageable costs. Technological advances were shifting to measuring DNA, protein and chromatin modifications and their multimodal combinations in single cells, and early studies were combining technologies into streamlined workflows. Although ambitious, these combined technologies would generate a comprehensive resource that would be invaluable for biology and medicine4.To generate a high-quality atlas, it was important to align community standards and definitions from the start. Scientists upload genomic data and harmonized metadata directly into HCA’s data ecosystem, with tools available to ensure quality and alignment between datasets. The HCA’s Standards and Technology Working Group developed benchmarks and quality control measures for determining whether the data are suitable to construct a high-quality atlas5. At the time of the HCA launch, data handling and analysis were only beginning to be connected in end-to-end pipelines, and it was not yet possible to integrate multiple datasets — almost all studies analyzed one dataset at a time. But it soon became apparent that it was not possible to successfully analyze single-cell data variation with fixed pipelines and parameters, prompting the HCA to instead set broad standards that each organ, tissue or system needed to meet; tailored data collection strategies; and later, integration methods to meet the characteristics and needs of individual organs. Importantly, the HCA established the structure for making cell annotations comparable across datasets and offered useful online tools like the Cell Annotation Platform for the entire community to use.A major challenge was that, in dissociating a tissue into single cells for sequencing, information about the cell’s original location within the tissue was lost. Several 2016 studies helped to overcome this hurdle. One approach provided a way to measure the spatial distribution of transcripts by annealing fixed tissue samples to barcoded reverse transcriptase primers, which enabled quantitative transcriptomics while keeping positional information6. This new ‘spatial transcriptomics’ and other imaging technologies added a new dimension to the type of data accruing in cell atlases by providing the physical locations of cells in tissues. But the data still needed to be integrated with sequencing data from dissociated cells to deliver single-cell resolution and/or full transcriptome coverage, and the HCA took on this critical challenge. The HCA defined how to test, optimize, benchmark and further develop foundational spatial transcriptomics methods for its integrated atlas-scale projects. Today, spatial technologies can map thousands of RNAs simultaneously and can incorporate protein, metabolite and lipid locations within a cell or large tissue area.By 2020, the HCA had generated or incorporated detailed maps of numerous human organs and tissues, including the lung and the liver, and by 2024 the HCA community had launched four integrated v1 HCA atlases: the Human Lung Cell Atlas (HLCA) v.1 (ref. 7), whole-brain and cortical atlases from the NIH BRAIN Initiative8, and the Human Retina Cell Atlas v.1 (ref. 9). Importantly, the HCA framework enabled researchers and existing consortia to submit their own datasets for integration into these bigger initiatives. For example, an early molecular cell atlas of the lung used droplet- and plate-based single-cell RNA-seq of 75,000 cells to define the gene expression profiles and anatomical locations in 58 different cell populations10. The integrated HLCA v.1 contains over 2 million cells from the respiratory tracts of 486 individuals, from 49 different datasets generated by the research community at large.The initial atlases are already showing their impact. At first the data provided researchers with robust normal references for disease studies. More recently the clinical benefit has started to be realized. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the HCA data from millions of cells allowed scientists to identify the tissues expressing genes relevant for SARS-CoV-2 viral entry and activation and to understand epidemiological factors associated with the disease11. The HLCA includes data from patients with lung disease, showing variation between healthy individuals and genetic comparisons of different diseases like COVID-19, cancer or fibrosis, but more work is needed to identify how these data can be used for therapeutic discovery. Researchers now are looking deeply at a specific gene program or cell type of interest, identifying drug targets and biomarkers for better diagnosis or therapeutics.This is where the field is heading now: from primarily a map of individual cells with some 2D spatial information, it is expanding toward integrated 3D, multimodal maps of entire organs and eventually the human body. To get there, even more technologies will need to be developed, to address existing problems and others that have not been imagined yet. The next phase, HCA 2.0, will focus on extending the atlas in several directions — tackling spatial and multimodal data and covering a wider variety of age, geographic and ethnic diversity. It will include a more systematic focus on specific diseases, beyond the representative healthy data it now includes.AI models will be at the heart of the HCA 2.0 — in fact, the HCA has provided much of the cell and tissue data used to train the foundation models deployed by the research community today. These AI models learn from the millions of previously annotated cells to classify new cells on the basis of their molecular profiles and perform many other tasks. Multimodal foundation models will also integrate diverse data modalities, including DNA, epigenetics, proteins, spatial localization, routine clinical imaging and clinical information. At the same time, agentic AI is increasingly allowing a new generation of data analysis. Autonomous agents are using skills from the HCA playbook to enable faster analyses, especially those for single-cell and spatial data that still are not automated well. Further, AI can identify patterns in vast and complex datasets that researchers may not anticipate. Perturbational studies, human genetics and longitudinal data will enable AI models to predict, at scale, what will happen when a cell changes — for example, when a gene is deleted or when a cell is exposed to a drug — transforming the HCA from a static map into a predictive model of human biology12. The goal is to turn the reference atlas into something that researchers and clinicians can query and act on — a true virtual tissue model.The HCA now has over 4,000 members from more than 100 countries, with connections and partnerships with many consortia and organizations (including the Kidney Precision Medicine Project, the NIH BRAIN Initiative, the Hemsley Charitable Trust, LungMAP and UNESCO). From the beginning, they have been committed to creating an open and globally representative atlas for humanity worldwide, with HCA regional groups emerging over the past decade in Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East. This has meant creating a coordinated community effort for participating scientists with diverse funding sources. HCA 2.0 will increase the global community’s representation, and last year the HCA’s Genetic Diversity Task Force established metrics for doing so. The diseases they will choose to focus on will strongly align with the needs of low- and middle-income countries.Generating an atlas of 10 billion cells and creating virtual tissue models over the next decade is ambitious, but the HCA has a strong track record in coordinating grass roots input with strong leadership, working effectively across disciplines and sharing data and tools. Looking back, the HCA’s significance is not simply the number of cells mapped or datasets generated; its deeper ambition is to provide a new reference point for understanding what it means to be human at the most fundamental biological level. As Regev and Teichmann write, we all must be proud of the role the HCA has played “in establishing a playbook for what big, international science that is open to anyone who adheres to a shared set of values can look like in biomedicine in the post-Human Genome Project era.”
